title: When Tokyo's Doctors Decided to Make Their Own Thermometers
dek: In 1921 a struggling thermometer maker asked a doctor for help, and Japan's physicians answered by founding the company that became Terumo.

story.founder: Shibasaburo Kitasato, Miozo Sasagawa and fellow physicians
story.company: Sekisen Ken-onki, the Red Line Thermometer Corporation (later Terumo)
story.event: Physicians founding a company to take over a failing thermometer works
story.summary: With imported clinical thermometers scarce in Japan after the First World War, the engineer Eiji Takeuchi's thermometer works ran short of money and he asked Dr Miozo Sasagawa of the Tokyo Medical Association for help. Sasagawa proposed that physicians found a company of their own to take over the business; Shibasaburo Kitasato chaired its founding meeting on 17 September 1921. The Red Line Thermometer Corporation sold its first thermometer in February 1922 and was renamed Terumo in 1974.
paragraphs: On 17 September 1921, Shibasaburo Kitasato took the chair at the founding meeting of a small company in Tokyo. He was then chairman of the Japan Medical Association and the country's best-known bacteriologist, trained in Robert Koch's laboratory in Berlin, where he had grown the tetanus bacillus in pure culture and helped found serum therapy. The new firm, registered with capital of 500,000 yen, had a narrow purpose: to make accurate clinical thermometers in Japan.

The need had been building for years. German thermometers had dominated the Japanese market, and once the First World War broke out in 1914, the company's own history says, Japan faced critical shortages. Doctors were asking for a good domestic instrument. An engineer, Eiji Takeuchi, had been making and selling thermometers at his own works, but the business ran into financial trouble. He turned to an acquaintance, Dr Miozo Sasagawa, chairman of the Tokyo Medical Association.

Sasagawa knew how much doctors needed thermometers they could trust. What he proposed was a company: physicians would set up a maker of their own to carry on Takeuchi's business. He asked Kitasato's opinion. Kitasato agreed, signed the founding prospectus as a supporter and chaired the meeting. He is reported to have said that he had never before involved himself in a commercial company, and accepted because these thermometers were for medicine. Doctors alone could not run a business, so Hiroshi Morishita, the businessman behind the Jintan medicine brand, joined the board as an adviser. Sasagawa became the first president of Sekisen Ken-onki, the Red Line Thermometer Corporation.

Its first thermometer went on sale in February 1922 under the Jintan name. Kitasato's place among the founders, one company history notes, helped the newcomer win credibility with doctors quickly. In 1936 it renamed itself Jintan Thermometer and became Japan's leading maker of clinical thermometers. For four decades thermometers were its only product; the second, in 1963, was Japan's first disposable syringe. In 1974 it took the name Terumo, which Takeuchi's works had carried, from the German word for thermometer. At its centenary in 2021 it employed more than 26,000 people.

quote.text: The mechanic, who wishes to do his work well, must first sharpen his tools. When you are living in any state, take service with the most worthy among its great officers, and make friends of the most virtuous among its scholars.
quote.source_title: The Analects of Confucius (from the Chinese Classics), tr. James Legge, Project Gutenberg eBook #3330
quote.connection: Confucius puts good tools and good company in the same breath. Takeuchi had the craft but not the means to keep going; he went to Sasagawa, and Sasagawa went to Kitasato. The instrument survived because each of them knew whose judgement to seek.

reflection: Takeuchi's works did not survive as his own. What survived was the work, because he told someone outside it that he was in trouble, and that person knew whom to ask next. Saying a business is struggling can feel like admitting it should not exist. Here it was the start of something sturdier.

You know from the bench that a result is only as good as the instrument behind it, and that no instrument calibrates itself. Judgement is similar. In a tired week, a colleague whose standards you trust can see what you have stopped noticing, if you let them look before the work is finished.

sources.supports: Origin of Terumo: critical thermometer shortages in Japan after the First World War broke out in 1914; engineer Eiji Takeuchi made and sold thermometers at Takeuchi Terumo Works, ran into financial problems and sought help from his acquaintance Dr Miozo Sasagawa, chairman of the Tokyo Medical Association; Sasagawa knew doctors needed high-quality thermometers, leading to a company to succeed Takeuchi's business; on 17 September 1921 Kitasato, chairman of the Japan Medical Association, led the first general meeting and Sasagawa became first president; second product was Japan's first disposable syringe in 1963; more than 26,000 associates by 2021

cross_checks.claim: The company was founded in September 1921 by physicians, with Kitasato chairing the founding meeting
The founding answered doctors' need for reliable thermometers when imported supplies became scarce around the First World War
The first thermometer went on sale in February 1922 under the Jintan name
Thermometers remained the only product until the disposable syringe of 1963, and the company was renamed Terumo in 1974

research_notes: The slate credited the founding to Kitasato and physicians. Terumo's own centenary release (January 2021) makes the initiators the engineer Eiji Takeuchi, whose thermometer works was in financial trouble, and Dr Miozo Sasagawa of the Tokyo Medical Association, with Kitasato chairing the first general meeting; NetIB-News (2020) says the Tokyo Medical Association president proposed the company and consulted Kitasato, who signed the prospectus and chaired. The story follows both. Timing of the shortage: Terumo's release ties critical shortages to the outbreak of war in 1914, while NetIB-News says German thermometers became hard to get after the war; the story says shortages followed the outbreak of war, attributed to the company's history, and that doctors were asking for a domestic instrument. Japanese Wikipedia notes thermometers were already made in Japan before 1921, so the story does not call this the first domestic maker. Kitasato's remark is reported in Japanese at second hand ('it is said') and is paraphrased, not quoted. Hiroshi Morishita's role (director and adviser) comes from NetIB-News only; Terumo's English sources do not mention him, though the Jintan brand name on the first thermometer is in all sources. Funding is set to 'unknown': the capital of 500,000 yen is in the securities-report history, but no source I could read says who subscribed it. Sasagawa's given name is romanised 'Miozo' by Terumo; Japanese readings of 三男三 vary. In 1921 the national body Kitasato chaired was formally the Greater Japan Medical Association, predecessor of the Japan Medical Association; the story uses Terumo's wording. The Encyclopedia.com directory entry contains small errors elsewhere in Kitasato's biography (for example the date of his Keio deanship), so it is used only for the company facts and his training under Koch. terumo.com and terumo.co.jp block automated requests, so Terumo's account is cited from its subsidiaries' sites. No outcome figures conflict; the 26,000 associates figure is the company's own, from its chairman in January 2021.
